summary: Yahweh assigns Aaron to speak for Moses and warns that Pharaoh will not heed the coming signs. Aaron’s rod swallows the rods of Egyptian magicians, but Pharaoh remains unmoved; at the Nile, the waters turn to blood, fish die, and Egyptians dig for drinkable water while the king again refuses to listen.
whyItMatters: The contest over who will be heard moves from words to signs that affect ordinary people’s water supply. Pharaoh’s persistence is narrated alongside both divine hardening language and his own indifference to the damage.

context.author: Exodus names no writer of the finished book, though it depicts Moses writing particular words. Later tradition ascribes the Torah to him; its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through its story of rescue, covenant, and worship; this chapter names no narrower first audience.
context.date: The book gives a relative story sequence but no secure external year for the events. The dating and formation of its finished text remain debated.
context.setting: Pharaoh’s court and the Nile’s banks, with effects described across Egyptian water sources and households.
context.literaryForm: Commission, rival court sign, and the first extended plague report with warning, enactment, response, and duration.

before.text: Moses has repeated his fear that Pharaoh will not listen, after Israel itself could not hear the promise through anguish. Yahweh now specifies how Moses and Aaron will speak.

here.text: Aaron mediates the message; his rod defeats the court magicians’ signs, and the river’s transformation brings deaths of fish and loss of drinking water.

after.text: The following chapter brings frogs, lice, and flies, with Pharaoh briefly offering release and then retracting it when relief comes.

outline.heading: The speakers commissioned
outline.note: Aaron is assigned to relay Moses’ words and Pharaoh’s predicted refusal is announced.

outline.heading: Rods before Pharaoh
outline.note: Aaron’s rod becomes a serpent and swallows the magicians’ rods, yet Pharaoh does not listen.

outline.heading: A warning at the Nile
outline.note: Moses is to confront Pharaoh with the release demand and foretell foul, undrinkable water.

outline.heading: Water turned to blood
outline.note: Aaron stretches out his rod, fish die, and the magicians imitate the sign.

outline.heading: Indifference and a search for water
outline.note: Pharaoh leaves, Egyptians dig for water, and seven days pass after the river is struck.

keyVerses.text: The Egyptians shall know that I am Yahweh when I stretch out my hand on Egypt, and bring the children of Israel out from among them.”
keyVerses.why: The announced aim connects the judgments with Egypt recognizing Yahweh’s action.

keyVerses.text: The fish that were in the river died. The river became foul. The Egyptians couldn’t drink water from the river. The blood was throughout all the land of Egypt.
keyVerses.why: The dead fish and undrinkable river show what the sign costs beyond the court.

keyVerses.text: All the Egyptians dug around the river for water to drink; for they couldn’t drink the river water.
keyVerses.why: Ordinary Egyptians must dig for drinking water after Pharaoh turns away.

questions.question: In what sense is Moses “as God” to Pharaoh and Aaron his prophet?
questions.answer: The next verse explains the arrangement: Moses receives commands and Aaron speaks them to Pharaoh. The language describes a chain of authorized speech in this scene, not a claim that Moses has become a deity.

questions.question: What does this chapter say about hardening Pharaoh’s heart?
questions.answer: Yahweh says he will harden Pharaoh’s heart so signs and judgments multiply, Israel is brought out, and Egyptians know who he is. The narrator then reports hardened refusal after the signs, without resolving how divine action and the king’s responsibility relate.

questions.question: Why does Aaron’s rod swallowing the others matter?
questions.answer: Egyptian wise men reproduce the serpent sign, so the court sees more than one impressive act. Aaron’s rod swallows theirs, yet the narrative immediately says Pharaoh still does not listen.

questions.question: Does the text explain how the magicians imitate the signs?
questions.answer: It says they use enchantments and reproduce the rod sign and the blood sign, but gives no procedure or independent explanation of their power. Their imitation does not undo the effects on the river or persuade Pharaoh to release Israel.

questions.question: Why meet Pharaoh by the river?
questions.answer: Yahweh directs Moses to the riverbank where Pharaoh will be in the morning, with the rod from the earlier sign. The announced change to blood will affect the very water source at that meeting place.

questions.question: Who suffers when the Nile becomes undrinkable?
questions.answer: The fish die and Egyptians cannot drink from the river; they dig nearby for water. The passage shows a population bearing the cost of this confrontation and does not restrict the damage to Pharaoh alone.

questions.question: What are “wonders” and “judgments” in the opening speech?
questions.answer: They are the announced actions Yahweh will multiply in Egypt while bringing Israel out. The chapter’s rod and river scenes begin to give those broad terms visible consequences.

questions.question: How does Pharaoh respond after the river is struck?
questions.answer: The magicians duplicate the sign, Pharaoh’s heart remains hardened, and he returns home without taking the event to heart. Meanwhile other Egyptians search for drinkable water for seven days after the blow.

glossary.def: The unspecified methods by which Egyptian magicians imitate the reported signs.
The staff Aaron casts before Pharaoh and uses in the command over Egyptian waters.
The great acts announced against Egypt in connection with Israel’s release.
